blocks.text: Stephen’s long speech retells Israel’s history in a hostile hearing and moves toward his accusation in verses 51–53. Acts presents speeches as literary compositions within ancient narrative rather than word-for-word transcripts; they may preserve traditions, but they should not be read as courtroom stenography. This means the speech’s shaping and argument matter alongside the events it recounts.

Verses 42–43 quote a Greek form of Amos 5:25–27 in Stephen’s account of Israel’s worship history. The names rendered Moloch and Rephan belong to that Greek textual tradition. The corresponding names in other textual forms of Amos are difficult to identify with confidence, so they should not be casually harmonized or used to make claims about later peoples or groups.

Questions about Acts’ historical reliability are best considered claim by claim, comparing particular details with independent evidence rather than treating the whole book as either automatically reliable or automatically unreliable.

Stephen’s speech is rhetoric spoken by a character before hostile council members. Its sharp language about ancestral resistance should not be turned into blanket blame against all Jews. Acts also survives in textual witnesses with differing profiles, including a substantially distinctive form often called the Western text; individual differences require case-by-case judgment.
